title: SPINAL MUSCULAR ATROPHY WITH CONGENITAL BONE FRACTURES 2

relationships.phenotype: SPINAL MUSCULAR ATROPHY WITH CONGENITAL BONE FRACTURES 2

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that spinal muscular atrophy with congenital bone fractures-2 (SMABF2) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the ASCC1 gene (614215) on chromosome 10q22.1.

checks.claim: Spinal muscular atrophy with congenital bone fractures-2 (SMABF2) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the ASCC1 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: We identified homozygous and compound-heterozygous nonsense and frameshift TRIP4 and ASCC1 mutations that led to a truncation or the entire absence of the respective proteins and cosegregated with the disease phenotype.
checks.explanation: The abstract supports recessive homozygous/compound heterozygous ASCC1 mutations causing the SMA with bone fractures phenotype. However, it pools the zygosity findings for TRIP4 and ASCC1, so it doesn't say which zygosities occurred in ASCC1. The name 'SMABF2' is not used.

checks.claim: The ASCC1 gene is located on chromosome 10q22.1.
checks.evidence_quote: We report on recessive loss-of-function mutations in two genes (TRIP4 and ASCC1) that encode subunits of the nuclear activating signal cointegrator 1 (ASC-1) complex.
checks.explanation: The chromosomal location is standard nomenclature for the gene the paper names. The abstract does not itself state 10q22.1.

paragraphs.text: Spinal muscular atrophy with congenital bone fractures-2 is a severe autosomal recessive neuromuscular disorder that starts before birth. Features include prenatal-onset muscle weakness, neonatal hypotonia, arthrogryposis, congenital bone fractures, and respiratory insufficiency. Oliveira et al. (2017) placed the disorder within the spectrum of spinal muscular atrophy or primary muscle disease. ASCC1 encodes a subunit of the activating signal cointegrator-1 (ASC-1) complex, a transcriptional coactivator made of 4 subunits: ASCC1, ASCC2, ASCC3, and TRIP4 (Böhm et al., 2019).

checks.claim: Spinal muscular atrophy with congenital bone fractures-2 is a severe autosomal recessive neuromuscular disorder with prenatal onset.
checks.evidence_quote: Whole-exome sequencing was performed with variant filtering assuming a recessive disease model.
checks.explanation: The paper describes a severe neuromuscular disorder with a recessive model and congenital fractures. It does not state prenatal onset or 'autosomal' explicitly.

checks.claim: Features of spinal muscular atrophy with congenital bone fractures-2 include prenatal-onset muscle weakness, neonatal hypotonia, arthrogryposis, congenital bone fractures, and respiratory insufficiency.
checks.evidence_quote: The patient presented generalized hypotonia, congenital bone fractures, lack of spontaneous movements and poor respiratory effort.
checks.explanation: Hypotonia, fractures and respiratory problems are described. Prenatal-onset muscle weakness and arthrogryposis are not mentioned in the abstract.

checks.claim: Oliveira et al. (2017) placed spinal muscular atrophy with congenital bone fractures-2 within the spectrum of spinal muscular atrophy or primary muscle disease.
checks.evidence_quote: This confirms ASCC1 involvement in a severe neuromuscular disease lying within the spinal muscular atrophy or primary muscle disease spectra.

checks.claim: ASCC1 encodes a subunit of the activating signal cointegrator-1 (ASC-1) complex, a transcriptional coactivator.
checks.evidence_quote: The activating signal cointegrator 1 (ASC-1) complex acts as a transcriptional coactivator for a variety of transcription factors and consists of four subunits: ASCC1, ASCC2, ASCC3 and TRIP4.

checks.claim: The ASC-1 complex is made of 4 subunits: ASCC1, ASCC2, ASCC3, and TRIP4.
checks.evidence_quote: consists of four subunits: ASCC1, ASCC2, ASCC3 and TRIP4.

paragraphs.text: Böhm et al. (2019) gave a clinical, histologic, and genetic description of 3 further families with ASCC1 mutations. All patients had severe prenatal-onset muscle weakness, neonatal hypotonia, arthrogryposis, and congenital bone fractures. Muscle biopsies from affected infants showed intense oxidative rims beneath the sarcolemma and scattered sarcomere remnants with enlarged Z-bands. The authors suggested that these findings may be a histopathologic hallmark of the disorder.

paragraphs.text: Oliveira et al. (2017) performed whole-exome sequencing under a recessive model in a female newborn with SMABF2. They found no disease-causing variants in genes known to cause congenital myopathies, muscle diseases, or other neuromuscular disorders. They did identify a homozygous frameshift mutation in the ASCC1 gene (c.157dupG; Glu53GlyfsTer19), which made her the second reported case.

paragraphs.text: In a stillborn infant with SMABF2, Giuffrida et al. (2020) identified compound heterozygous mutations in the ASCC1 gene. Microarray analysis first detected a microdeletion of about 64 kb that removed 4 exons of ASCC1. Exome analysis then found a c.1027C-T transition that produced an arg343-to-ter (R343X) substitution, introducing a premature termination codon. The authors stated that this was the first reported case of ASCC1 compound heterozygosity due to an exonic microdeletion together with a nucleotide variant. They suggested that exonic copy number variants are an underestimated cause of disease alleles.

paragraphs.text: Knierim et al. (2016) found that ASCC1-mutant fibroblasts downregulated genes linked to neurogenesis, neuronal migration, and pathfinding (SERPINF1, DAB1, SEMA3D, and SEMA3A) and genes linked to bone development (TNFRSF11B, RASSF2, and STC1). Immunoprecipitation of the ASC-1 complex consistently copurified the transcriptional cofactor CSRP1. In 17.5-day mouse embryos, Trip4 and Ascc1 had identical expression patterns, with high expression in spinal cord, brain, paraspinal ganglia, thyroid, and submandibular glands. The authors concluded that dysfunction of a transcriptional coactivator complex can cause a syndrome affecting the neuromuscular system.
